General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Solidjs ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Solid 2.0

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Solidjs

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that 5 years is a long time to work on anything.
  • Solid 1.0 made a bet that fine-grained reactivity, signals, was the right foundation for building user interfaces.
  • Sources indicate that more recently that conversation has shifted to AI, arguably an even larger change in how we build.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that 5 years is a long time to work on anything. It took 5 years from my first commit of Solid to 1.0, and it's been another 5 since then.

A lot changes in 5 years. Solid 1.0 made a bet that fine-grained reactivity, signals, was the right foundation for building user interfaces. Back then it was an unusual position. Today signals are everywhere. In Angular, in Svelte's runes, in Vue Vapor, and in a proposal before TC39 to put them in the language itself. It even pushed the conversation into React's compiler.

Sources indicate that more recently that conversation has shifted to AI, arguably an even larger change in how we build. But Solid has always been about building the right things; the performant things. So for us the mission hasn't really changed all that much. The things that we identified as standout about our approach still stand out now. But instead of living in the shadow of more popular solutions Solid 2.0 carves out a path that others can follow. Deliberately this time.

Today that solution reaches stable.

If fine-grained reactivity's greatest strength is knowing the shape of our application, that knowledge shouldn't end with the process, or the machine the code is running on. Real applications are distributed. Real applications are born from data that lives on a server. The coordination of these pieces should be intentional and by design.

This starts with bringing async into the graph. A computation can return a Promise or an async iterator, and everything downstream just understands:.

This allows authoring by affordance while automating the handling of race conditions. The introduction of async doesn't cause an app refactor. Speculative state is automatically rolled back without manually written processes ensuring the server remains the authority on truth.

SolidStart introduce the world to server functions in early 2022, and now they have found their way home to Solid's core, better than ever. Not only do they support highly capable RPC calls over Request/Response but persistent connections over Server Sent Events. And consuming it remains as simple as the code below.

This is only the beginning of what can be done with Server Functions and we will be announcing some new features (like reactive Server Components) in coming weeks that leverage this capability.

"But, we aren't writing the code anymore!" We hear you. A system built on constraints by construction ends up with less code to maintain and less edge cases. What used to be considered a DX shortcoming of reactive frameworks are now their greatest strength. And Solid 2.0 goes all in.

Every framework now says it "works great with AI", and usually that means models have seen a lot of it. That's a statement about training data, not about the framework. The question that matters is what happens when the agent gets it wrong.

In most frameworks a reactive mistake is silent. The app runs, it's just wrong, and the framework can't tell you, because it can't see it either. Solid can. A fine-grained graph knows exactly what was read, where, and what will upgrade. So Solid 2.0's development builds report mistakes as they happen, with a stable code, the location in your source, and the fix:.

These handle everything from strict errors to helpful heuristics. Thanks to async in the graph we can detect waterfalls, poorly constructed effect loops, poorly scaling graph shapes like wide graph fanouts and fan-ins. Today along with linting rules we can provide the best in class direction for agents at compile and at runtime.

In a recent development, this area is still evolving as we learn more about how agents build applications with Solid. The hard part, defining the primitives and semantics, is done. We've integrated with new dev tooling, and Chrome's Performance Tracks. And this capability goes beyond development as this observability powers things like our updated Sentry plugin so you can get the same information on your production builds.

Sources indicate that we've also been looking at alternative syntax. Solid 2.0 adds experimental support for ReactiveScript and TSRX, both aiming to use compilation to further improve agent authoring.

According to recent reports, I've always been a major believer that React's super power is its composability. That it allowed the ecosystem to build on its humble pieces. However, we've learned a lot since 2013. At that point composable state, async patterns, and server rendering lacked the primitives to build upon and the ecosystem came up with their own solutions. This was fine for a while but tied React's hands and fractured their ecosystem. Something only a framework as popular as React could survive.

Recent findings suggest that newer frameworks have taken more on themselves and tend to only have one metaframework, or one router. We respect React's original positioning but have updated it for 2026. It isn't about restricting the solution but giving developers the primitives to build upon in the way React originally did. Server functions are example of this. Supporting any router, and cache solution for Single-Flight Mutation is another.

It has been revealed that we retired our metaframework SolidStart, since every primitive needed to build a Solid Metaframework is now provided by the core or by framework agnostic Vite plugins. We believe that building an opinionated layer like a metaframework shouldn't have you needing to re-implement everything again. We've taken care of the hard parts so you can focus on what you care about. And these days a lot of that work is going to be taken on by your agent. This means less to maintain but no loss in capability.

And this makes it easier for the ecosystem. Solid 2.0 only requires one Clerk or Sentry plugin since we provide the primitives for Request/Response (built on web standards) and the hooks for observability that work across any library. We've already seen success with TanStack Query and Router being as capable as anything we've built first party, bringing in Tanner's impeccable attention to detail for the APIs people love to use.

It has been revealed that somehow even though Solid 2.0 brings more capability to Solid, we've collapsed the surface area at almost every point. There are less primitives needed to be learnt, less ceremony around handling async. createResource, batch, startTransition, on, produce, createComputed, createMutable are all gone, because we no longer need them.

Sources indicate that the equivalent code written for Solid 2.0 is shorter and clearer on intent. It informs our ability observe the runtime, provide better compiler errors, and removes the need for as many escape hatches (like createEffect) that can get us in trouble. This is something we believe key in an age of AI. Safe by construction rather than by exhaustion. Reduce complexity by deriving(reducing) state rather than putting it in a reducer.

When the framework carries the guarantees, all loading state, race conditions, and cancellation logic disappears and what you are left with is the UI.

The first discussions of what a Solid 2.0 would look like started at the moment 1.0 was released. We saught feedback from the community on latest reactivity ideas. The real effort started in late 2024. We unveiled the road to 2.0 in February 2025. Over a year of experiments followed, rewriting the reactive core from scratch until the async model held up to everything we threw at it. The beta landed in March, and the Release Candidate in August, with the API frozen.

It has been revealed that then 23 release candidates in 14 weeks. In that time alone, 971 pull requests were merged and 753 issues closed. We set one bar for stable. A full week with no regression in ordinary app code, and no crash or hang anywhere. It took a while to get there. By the end, the bug reports coming in were from people(agents) deliberately hunting edge cases in the deepest corners of the scheduler, and finding them.

So many people have touched the project over the past 5 years, from working on the initial reactivity prototypes, to testing the latest RC builds on their production apps. I've tried to thank as many of you as I can and attached hundreds of handles in the RC announcement. There are so many. There are also the many great organizations that have sponsored our development over the years: Sentry, Netlify, Google Chrome, JetBrains, Anomaly, Cursor, Code Rabbit, Anthropic, Tembo and so many more.

Sources indicate that but mostly I want to thank everyone who has believed in the project. We've accomplished great things and there is much more to come. That isn't possible without all of you. Personally, the past 2 and half years have been some of the most difficult of my life, but knowing what we are building that impacts so many people leaves me with a sense of fulfillment. Solid has always been bigger than its core team, and 2.0 is the clearest proof of that yet.

It has been revealed that solid 2.0 is here. Let's build.

Sources indicate that the Long Hold refers to a diagnostic warning in Solid 2.0. It fires when a hold has been shown(isPending) but sufficient time has passed since the last input. Holds were at the heart of our async work for 2.0, and we acknowledge it took a while for this all to land.

These Are the Best Ways to Encrypt Your Email

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that you probably already know that your email isn't actually all that private, especially if you have a free account with a major service provider like Gmail (Google) or Outlook (Microsoft).
  • As this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server.
  • Emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that you probably already know that your email isn't actually all that private, especially if you have a free account with a major service provider like Gmail (Google) or Outlook (Microsoft). But if you are sending sensitive information via email, you can minimize what can be snooped on and by whom using end-to-end encryption, which generally ensures that only the recipient can read your message. Here's what you need to know about email encryption and how to set up an extra layer of privacy.

As this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

Emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

It has been revealed that by contrast, with end-to-end encryption (E2EE), emails are readable only on the sender's and recipient's devices, and can be decrypted only with the recipient's private key. They're never translated into plaintext as they pass between and through servers to their destination, meaning that no one—including server providers, hackers, or law enforcement—can view the content. It's worth noting, though, that E2EE is not impenetrable nor a total guarantee of privacy. For example, metadata like subject lines and email addresses may remain in plaintext, and encrypted messages are still susceptible to phishing. Plus, forwarding an encrypted message breaks the encryption.

Still, end-to-end encryption is especially useful when sending sensitive information that may be valuable to bad actors, though if security and privacy are a high priority, you may want to consider it for all of your emails. How you deploy encryption depends on whether you are adding it to your current email or switching to a dedicated provider.

Recent findings suggest that if you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail users in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise customers of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

In a recent development, for those who are willing to start fresh with a upcoming email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between consumers on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.

The bottom line here is that email wasn't designed to be a highly secure form of communication. End-to-end encryption does add a layer of privacy and security if you jump through hoops to set it up, but it's still susceptible to human error and social engineering.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: 10 Privacy Hacks Every Mac User Should Know

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that apple has a pretty good track record on privacy.
  • Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device.
  • Industry observers note that another hack for maintaining privacy on public networks is to enable rotating MAC addresses, which randomizes the identifier your device broadcasts when scanning for and connecting to wifi.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that apple has a pretty good track record on privacy. The tech giant bakes a number of protections into its OSes to keep your data from being shared or stolen. That remarked, you can make your Apple devices even more secure. There are plenty of opt-in settings that make it even harder for anyone to snoop on your device and activity. These are the best privacy hacks for your Mac.

Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

Industry observers note that another hack for maintaining privacy on public networks is to enable rotating MAC addresses, which randomizes the identifier your device broadcasts when scanning for and connecting to wifi. If you use either your real MAC address or a fixed one (random but unchanging), it's easier to track your activity on that network, including when you arrive, how long you stay, and when you leave. Rotating addresses are best for public, shared networks you temporarily connect to, and don't require a login via a captive portal (like hotel wifi). You can turn this on for specific networks via Settings > Wi-Fi > [Network Name] > Details and change Private Wi-Fi address to Rotating.

According to recent reports, images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for rapidly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.).

Apple collects information about your device for diagnostic purposes or to improve apps and services, some of which is shared with third-party app developers. This may include crash and usage data as well as recordings and transcripts of Siri interactions and iCloud analytics. You can disable sharing for some or all of these categories under Settings > Privacy & Security > Analytics & Improvements.

You may be surprised by the number of apps and system services that use your device's location in the background. You should definitely disable location services for third-party apps that don't require location to function. You can find these toggles under Settings > Privacy & Security > Location Services. You can also turn off location permissions for some Apple apps and services if you're not using them on your device, like Weather and Maps. Finally, tap System Services and disable location for any non-essential features—at the very least, disable "Mac Analytics" and "Significant Locations & routes" (which lets your Mac and other iCloud devices learn locations and routes you use often).

Industry observers note that third-party apps on your Mac that need access to your device's camera and microphone have to request permission, and it's easy to grant this in the moment and then forget that you've allowed it. You should regularly audit which apps have these permissions and revoke access from those that don't need them on a day-to-day basis. Disabling them forces the app to ask again. Go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone or Camera to see the allowed apps and flip the toggle to disable permissions.

Another permission type you may have granted without much thought is local network access. This allows third-party apps to discover and communicate with other devices—printers, smart speakers, and IoT devices—on your home wifi. While this may be useful for services like Spotify that cast to connected hardware, other utilities, media apps, and games probably don't need to be mapping your network in the background. Go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Local Network to audit permissions and disable those that aren't needed.

Sources indicate that another important permission to check concerns third-party apps that have access to your Mac's full disk, which includes data from Mail, Messages, Safari, Home, Time Machine, and admin settings. If an app only works with files you explicitly open and save, it doesn't need full disk access. Legitimate use cases may include antivirus and malware scanners, productivity tools, or backup utilities that you trust. You can also audit which apps have access to specific files and folders. This is under Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access or Files & Folders.

If you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the last year, PC builders have been force-fed a very specific narrative about why buying a computer required a second mortgage.
  • And when news of a class action lawsuit against Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron broke in June, I was jubilant but fully expecting it to go nowhere, as this AI build-out was a good cover and the case hung on a “well, they’ve done it before” kind of prosecution.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the last year, PC builders have been force-fed a very specific narrative about why buying a computer required a second mortgage. We were told that the AI data center boom was sucking up all the memory — resulting in 500% price surges.

And when news of a class action lawsuit against Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron broke in June, I was jubilant but fully expecting it to go nowhere, as this AI build-out was a good cover and the case hung on a “well, they’ve done it before” kind of prosecution.

But after a motion to dismiss got denied by the judge, who compared their synchronized supply starvation to “hawks flying in formation,” and the devastating newly introduced leaks about alleged GPU and memory shortage engineering, it’s becoming clear that something stinks.

This whole “RAMageddon” crisis is starting to feel like a deliberate squeeze rather than natural market evolution, and the fact that this entire artificial house of cards is currently collapsing under federal scrutiny is my definition of hopecore.

The significant three memory makers — Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron — have been fighting this massive antitrust lawsuit alleging they formed an illegal oligopoly to artificially inflate DRAM prices.

Their defense was entirely predictable: they filed a motion to dismiss, claiming that their identical supply cuts were just the natural, independent reactions of companies surviving in a changing market.

And this week, Judge Noël Wise completely rejected that defense.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Judge Wise (which is a very apt last name) explicitly states that the plaintiff’s evidence is highly plausible following a staggering 500% price surge. The ruling highlighted that this wasn’t just a case of market leader leading and other following; it was a highly coordinated structural shift.

According to the court’s findings, the significant three allegedly halted consumer DDR4 manufacturing and restricted general DRAM supply under the guise of an HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) data center pivot, while simultaneously adopting identical, highly unusual vetting procedures to verify end-customer demand.

Like my nephew who just got into playing Among Us indicates: "sus".

The Judge cited past legal precedent describing oligopolies as competitors watching each other “like hawks,” but noted this goes far beyond observation — ruling their synchronized supply starvation resembles “hawks flying in formation.” The companies now have until December 7 to officially respond to the complaint.

While the memory giants were allegedly fixing the RAM market, an entirely different kind of market manipulation has been allegedly happening on the GPU front.

In the fallout of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, a damning latest report alleges that the AI hardware shortage wasn’t driven by insatiable demand, but by an attempt to hide a massive oversupply. According to the leaks, Huang feared that Nvidia had over-ordered from TSMC and was about to be stuck with a mountain of excess enterprise silicon.

According to recent reports, instead of letting the market naturally correct (which would have dropped GPU prices), it’s alleged that Huang engaged in a massive “circular financing” scheme. Nvidia used its own capital to fund smaller neocloud AI startups, effectively paying them to absorb Nvidia’s excess GPUs.

It was an artificial demand loop, convincing the broader market that the AI hardware frenzy was still booming and keeping margins astronomically bloated across the industry.

Recent findings suggest that notably, the leaks vindicate current interim CEO Colette Kress. Rather than co-authoring the shortage, Kress, in her role as CFO, reportedly viewed the circular financing practice as highly toxic, actively challenging Huang’s bets and urging him to slow down.

This is why the RAMageddon Reset matters, and why you should absolutely refuse to pay inflated prices this Black Friday.

It has been revealed that the exorbitant cost of PC gaming in 2026 wasn’t driven by an unstoppable technological revolution — more and more, it’s becoming clear that it was driven by white-collar collusion. But that era is over.

Smuggling rings and circular financing deals are being exposed and dismantled. And now, a federal judge is forcing Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron to answer for their synchronized price gouging.

In a recent development, the artificial floor holding up the PC hardware market has been kicked out from underneath their feet. As these companies scramble to avoid massive federal antitrust fines and DOJ indictments, they will be forced to flood the market with the supply they have been hoarding.

In a recent development, hold the line, keep your wallet closed, and watch those prices fall. My prediction is still in play.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updates are generally good for your devices. The latest Chrome update, for example, patches an actively exploited security vulnerability, while Apple's latest updates stop people from seeing iMessages they shouldn't have access to. In most cases, it's beneficial to update your tech to the latest software version whenever possible.

In a recent development, sadly, updates aren't all perfect, as Google Pixel users are discovering this week. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November patch apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

Here's the situation: Following the November update, some users are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the issue is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal matter. It's not like all Pixel users are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

Luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some owners are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

In a recent development, what does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

If your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November update, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the problem does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this week, Apple started shipping the HomeView, its first display made for the smart home. On the HomeView, there’s one particularly nice feature that I’d love to see make its way to all Apple platforms: Ambient Dark Mode.

It has been revealed that on iOS, iPadOS, and macOS today – the only flexibility you have on dark mode is whether or not it automatically switches on towards night time. While this is generally helpful and certainly appreciated, it isn’t super granular. Of course, you can adjust the time when it switches, but generally speaking its just a one time toggle.

With HomeView, you can enable ambient dark mode. In display settings, once you enable automatic dark mode, there’s the usual two settings you’d see on other Apple platforms: sunrise to sunset, as well as a custom schedule. HomeView takes it a step further with ambient mode, where the ambient light sensor determines whether or not you should be in light or dark mode.

Of course, a sunrise to sunset schedule generally works for most cases. However, if you’re up late at night with your lights turned on, you still might prefer light mode in an instance where macOS would generally be in dark mode. Similarly, if you wake up later in the day with your curtains shut, at say 11am, you might not want to immediately see light mode on your phone the second you open your eyes.

There are tons of good reasons for why someone would prefer ambient light-based automatic light and dark mode switching. HomeView software is the first Apple platform to enable this, and I’d love to see it come to iPhone, iPad, and Mac starting next year with OS 28.

#27748. Claude was trained on protein sequences at scale

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2327 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Xinmingtu ↗ Open Full Page

Claude was trained on protein sequences at scale

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2327 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Xinmingtu

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A next-amino-acid test on little-studied proteins finds that the latest Claude models were trained on protein sequences at scale.
  • The latest Claude models were trained on protein sequences, at scale.
  • Frontier LLMs have started to look good at protein tasks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A next-amino-acid test on little-studied proteins finds that the latest Claude models were trained on protein sequences at scale. Other frontier models show no sign of it.

The latest Claude models were trained on protein sequences, at scale. Give Claude Fable 5.2 or Claude Opus 5.5 the start of a little-studied bacterial protein and they predict the next amino acid. Shuffle the protein and they can’t. No other model we tested can do this. Like a protein language model, they do better on bigger protein families, and they do it even in families with no papers at all. Fable 5.2 beats every open protein language model we ran, and Opus 5.5 is level with ProtGPT3-10B, the largest of them.

Update, 18 November 2026. Since the first version:.

Frontier LLMs have started to look good at protein tasks. Atharv Jayprakash highlighted GPT-6 Astra ranking SOD1 variants as well as ESM-2, and PG-LLM found the same across many proteins. Did these models learn from protein sequence databases such as UniProt, or from what is written about proteins?

In a recent development, famous proteins can’t tell the two apart: GFP is printed in countless papers, and most frontier models recite it. So we tested proteins that almost nobody writes about.

We give a model the start of a protein and ask for the next amino acids. Then we ask again on a shuffled copy of the same protein. Shuffling keeps the letters and destroys their order, so the difference in accuracy measures what the model knows about the sequence itself.

The test set is 668 bacterial and archaeal proteins from 167 Pfam families of unknown function. No family has a solved structure or more than three papers, and no protein has a close relative in UniProt. Each protein is cut at five points. At each cut the model writes the next 10 amino acids, and we score the first. Thinking is at its lowest setting. Appendix E has the details.

Fable 5.2 gets the next amino acid right 54% of the time on real proteins and 9% on shuffled ones. The gap is there in nearly every family, not just a few easy ones. It appears in Opus 4.7, jumps in Opus 5.5, and jumps again in Fable 5.2. GPT, Gemini and the seven open-weight models (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Qwen 3.8, Kimi K3.1 Pro, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3, gpt-oss-120b and Nemotron 3 Ultra) stay near zero, even when they simply continue raw FASTA text, the way they were trained. The latest Claude models also write runs of correct residues that other models rarely manage (Appendix B).

In a recent development, protein language models learn only from sequences, so they are the natural yardstick. The closest to an LLM are the ones that read a protein left to right and predict the next residue: ProtGPT3, whose 10-billion-parameter version is the largest open one, and ProGen3, whose largest public version has 3 billion. On the same input, Fable 5.2 beats both by a wide margin. Opus 5.5 is level with ProtGPT3-10B and below ProGen3-3B.

It has been revealed that ESM models are trained to see both sides of a residue, so continuing from the left is harder for them. Appendix C has all nine models.

If the models learned from sequences, families with more sequences should be easier. To test this over a wide range, we added 90 smaller families, down to 20 proteins each, for 257 families in all.

It has been revealed that they are. Opus 5.5 rises with the two protein language models, ProtGPT3-10B and ProGen3-3B, which are trained on nothing but sequences. Fable 5.2 rises fastest and levels off at about 300 proteins per family. Earlier Claude models rise at a lower level, and GPT and Gemini stay near zero. The knowledge also carries over to proteins published after the training cutoff, with no close relative before it (Appendix G).

Two other explanations don’t fit:.

Famous proteins are a different story. Many models do well on them, and several recite hundreds of residues letter for letter (Appendix B), because these sequences are all over papers and the web. In a first round with famous and obscure proteins side by side, Gemini 4 Carbon was strong on the famous ones and dropped to almost nothing on the obscure ones. The latest Claude models and ProtGPT3-10B held up, and Fable 5.2 was the strongest on both.

In a recent development, this also explains the SOD1 and PG-LLM results. Ranking variants of a well-known protein can lean on what is written about it: which residues are buried, which substitutions break a helix, which mutations cause ALS. In PG-LLM, accuracy doesn’t depend on alignment depth and improves with more thinking, both signs of that route. Our test shuts it out. GPT-6 is good at the first kind of task and weak at the second; the latest Claude models are good at both.

The latest Claude models know protein families that almost nobody has studied. That takes a lot of sequence data, not a few examples: protein sequences were a sizeable part of their training. Opus 5.5 behaves like a protein language model, and Fable 5.2 goes beyond the best one we could run. GPT and Gemini show none of this. Whatever protein sequence they saw in training, it was not enough to learn these families.

Recent findings suggest that DNA is different. Opus 5.5 predicts human and mouse coding sequence but not the rest of the genome, and barely the bacterial genes behind the proteins it knows (Appendix A). It learned proteins, not genomes.

We are curious what else this knowledge supports. Fable 5.2 predicts little-studied proteins better than any open protein language model we ran, and protein language models carry more than next-residue statistics: ESM-2’s internal representations hold enough structure that a small folding module on top predicts 3D structures (ESMFold), and their probabilities rank the effects of mutations. Could Claude fold a protein, or rank its variants, the same way?

All code, test sets, model outputs and figures are in llm-bioseq-probe.

220-nucleotide windows, 200 shown and 20 to predict, from hg38, mm39 and the bacterial genes behind the test proteins, 500 per region. Non-coding windows contain no repeats, and the control shuffles each window keeping its dinucleotide counts. Opus 5.5 wrote all 20 nucleotides right 25 times in 500 human coding windows; a blind guess does that about once in a trillion. Gemini 4 Carbon blocks most DNA prompts before answering, so it is not shown.

All 10 residues right. Each question asks for the next 10 residues. On the 668 little-studied proteins, Claude Fable 5.2 gets all 10 right at 88 real cuts and Opus 5.5 at 12, and neither at any shuffled one. If their residues were independent guesses at their own per-residue accuracy, they would get 15.8 and 0.57 by chance.

Recent findings suggest that runs in a row. On shuffled proteins neither Fable 5.2 nor Opus 5.5 gets more than 3 residues in a row. Once on track they get surer: after one right residue, Opus 5.5 gets the next right 47% of the time, after four in a row 68%.

Recent findings suggest that reciting well-known proteins. At 158 points in well-studied proteins, each model was asked for the next 200 residues at once.

GPT-6.1 Sol never reaches 100 residues, and GPT-5.5 never gets past 2.

Choosing the proteins. We started from every Pfam family whose name says “domain of unknown function” (DUF) or “protein of unknown function”, and kept those with no structure in the PDB, at most 3 Europe PMC hits for the family’s accession, and at least 300 member proteins. We binned them by size (300 to 1,000 proteins, 1,000 to 3,000, 3,000 to 10,000, over 10,000) and drew 50 families per bin at random; only 17 families qualify above 10,000, so the set has 167. From each family we took 4 proteins from UniProt that are unreviewed (TrEMBL), come from Bacteria or Archaea, are 120 to 800 residues long, use only the 20 standard amino acids, are not low-complexity (Shannon entropy above 3.9 bits per residue), and are alone in their UniRef90 cluster, so no other UniProt protein is 90% or more identical to them. That gives 668 proteins.

Smaller families. For the family-size test we drew 30 more families in each of three smaller bins (20 to 60, 60 to 150 and 150 to 300 proteins) with the same criteria and 4 proteins per family, 360 proteins in all. Every model gets the same prompt and scoring as on the main set.

Cutting. Each protein is cut at 5 positions drawn at random inside its Pfam domain (the longest domain span, at least 40 residues), at least 10 residues from either end of the domain and with at least 30 residues before the cut: 3,340 cuts. Everything before the cut is the prefix; the residue right after it is the answer.

Sources indicate that asking. The model gets this message, with the prefix in 60-character lines (an example from one of the test proteins):.

Each model runs through its own API with temperature 0 where it is accepted, thinking off or at its lowest setting (for Opus 5.5 and the Fable models, low effort, at which the model still decides whether to think), no tools, and one sample per question. The Claude Fable models run through OpenRouter, since Anthropic’s API serves them only to workspaces that retain data. Models that declined to guess (GPT-4o, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM, gpt-oss) also got a version that adds “Give your best guess even if you are uncertain. Do not explain or refuse.”; those runs are marked separately.

Industry observers note that thinking. A reply counts as thought about when the API reports thinking tokens for it: thinking_tokens in Anthropic’s usage report, reasoning_tokens in OpenRouter’s. The thinking text itself is not kept; only the visible reply is scored. Fable 5.2 thought on 9% of questions, Opus 5.5 on 36%, Fable 5.1 never. Without thinking, Fable 5.2 is right 54.7% of the time on real proteins and 8.8% on shuffled ones (48.2% and 10.6% with thinking), and Opus 5.5 35.3% and 6.9% (34.1% and 8.6%).

Scoring. We read the last sequence the reply states: a run of capital amino-acid letters on its own line or after a label such as “Answer:”, skipping words, lists and anything inside thinking tags. If it starts by restating the end of the prefix, the restatement is dropped. Its first letter is the predicted next amino acid. A reply cut off at the length limit counts only if it opens with a sequence. Replies that state no sequence are excluded and counted (0.1% for Opus 5.5). Only the first residue is scored; the full 10 are used for exact continuations and runs. The same reader is used for every model and for real and shuffled proteins.

Recent findings suggest that the shuffled control. Each protein’s residues are shuffled once, with a random seed fixed by its accession, and the same 5 cut positions are asked on the shuffled sequence. The shuffle keeps the composition of the whole protein and destroys the order, so a model that knows only which amino acids are common scores the same on both.

Industry observers note that statistics. For each family we compute the share of correct first residues on real and on shuffled cuts, and take the difference, in percentage points. The result for a model is the mean of that gap over the 167 families. Intervals are 95% bootstraps over families (10,000 resamples), the main test is a one-sided sign-flip permutation test over families, and the family-size trend is the Spearman correlation between a family’s gap and the logarithm of its size.

Recent findings suggest that raw continuation. For models that allow it, the same prefix is sent without any instruction, as the text “>sequence” followed by the FASTA lines, through a plain completion endpoint (open-weight models on Fireworks) or as the start of the model’s own reply (Gemini 2.5 Pro). The first letter the model writes is scored as above.

It has been revealed that protein language models. They get the same prefix and no prompt. ProGen3, ProtGPT3, ProtGPT2 and Prot-xLSTM read it left to right and give a probability for the next token; the ESM models see the prefix, a mask in place of the next residue, and the end of the sequence. In every case the prediction is the most likely of the 20 standard amino acids.

Total API cost was about $730, plus a few dollars of GPU time for the protein language models.

Gemini 4 Carbon blocked about 75% of DNA prompts outright. OpenAI rejected 23 GPT-6 requests in the first round and 17 GPT-6.1 Sol requests in the main run as possible biological misuse, and 6.6% of GPT-6.2 Astra’s main-set questions (GPT-6.2 Sol: 0.6%). Claude Sonnet 4.5 refused 97% of requests that started its reply with a protein sequence, and Anthropic’s filter blocked 44% of Claude Fable 5’s questions as cyber content.

Leo Tianlai Chen built a set of 56 proteins from 31 of the families that were first made public in August 2026, after the assumed 1 July training cutoff, and have no earlier relative at 50% identity or more. The models cannot have seen them or anything close. Both Claude models still predict them, Fable 5.2 ahead of both protein language models, while GPT-6.2 Sol stays at zero. Every model scores about half of what it scores on the same families in the main set, as expected for proteins this distant. What the latest Claude models learned carries over to new members of a family.

The proteins were dated at their source, and none matches an earlier UniRef50 cluster at 50% identity or more. Cuts follow the main set’s rules. With 56 proteins only gaps of about 14 points or more are reliably detected, and the 1 July cutoff is an assumption.

Five Hacks Every Apple Watch Series 12 User Should Know

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The latest Apple Watches have a lot of newly introduced features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks.
  • The Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models.
  • You don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The latest Apple Watches have a lot of newly introduced features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks. While our general Apple Watch and fitness tracking hacks are still golden, Series 12 devices offer new features like native step counting, a Readiness app, an upgraded heart rate sensor, an AI-based version of Siri, and "audio intelligence" that can replay and summarize real-life conversations, within limits. Here's how to get the most out of them.

The Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models. Enjoy it! To add a step counter to your watch face, long-press on the clock screen to edit it, tap on a complication (that’s what Apple calls those little icons and numbers that appear on some watch faces), choose Activity, and then tap Steps.

You don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion. A button in your Apple Watch’s Control Center can turn the feature on and off. Keep it off except when you have a structured conversation that you’ll want to refer to later. This feature is currently in beta (which you can try now if you want to), but is expected to be available to everyone later this year.

According to recent reports, it's worth turning off the default setting not just because of the creepiness factor, but also because the recaps work best when there is a single subject of conversation, with a clear start and end, and just one context. If you leave recaps running all the time, your doctor’s appointment will get mixed in with your grocery shopping, YouTube watching, and everyday chatter.

According to recent reports, to finish off a recap and make it useful, take a look at the recap shortly after the conversation, tap the three-dots menu, and hit Edit. You’ll be able to adjust the notes and add your own notable details. Siri won’t identify speakers and seems to shy away from including certain details, like people’s names. You can add in what it missed and also create your own bullet points so that everything gets noted down while it’s still fresh in your mind.

This one isn’t specific to the Series 12, but if you haven’t gotten on board with the pinch and wrist flick gestures yet, now is a great time.

Industry observers note that first, the wrist flick: If a notification is on your screen, or you’re otherwise looking at something you’d rather be done with, just flick your wrist away from you and then back toward you, as if there were a crumb on the watch face and you wanted to knock it off. This will bring you back to the watch face and close whatever you were looking at.

Recent findings suggest that the double pinch is another useful one, although Apple calls it double tap. This is confusing because you aren’t double tapping the watch, you’re tapping your thumb and forefinger together while wearing the watch. You don’t need to touch the watch face at all. So, when you get a notification or a call, look at it on your watch, and pinch your thumb and forefinger (of the watch hand) together twice. The watch detects the pinch from subtle movements in your wrist, and it will open the notification. You can then use the wrist flick to close the notification. Performing a double pinch when no notification is on screen will bring up your smart stack. You can then double-pinch to move to the next card in the smart stack, or single-pinch to open that card and see its details.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to learn even more gestures, go into the Watch app, and select Accessibility and then Hand gestures. You can remap a whole-fist “clench” to do the same thing as pressing the digital crown, for example, or to open the control center or Siri.

A little rude, perhaps, but helpful: With the upcoming AI-based Siri, sometimes answers to questions can be long-winded. If Siri debuts into a novel-length response and you’re not interested in hearing all that, just put your palm over the screen. You’ll instantly be transported back to your watch face, and the Siri response will stop.

In a recent development, if you still want to see those longer responses without having Siri read the whole thing to you, you can set this up on your phone, and the settings will carry over to your watch. On your iPhone, go to Settings and tap Siri, then Responses. Select Silent responses instead of Spoken responses. You can then read through her answers, or skim them, as you prefer.

We wanted something that fit our lives, connected us as the Apple family we already are, and didn’t cost families a fortune.

It has been revealed that like most families, we had an old iPad lying around. We put it in a case with a magnet, stuck it to the fridge, and that became Milton.

The core organizer features are all available out of the box, but if you want to add more people to the app, sync across devices, or share the app with other family members (for their personal devices), you’ll need to purchase Milton Individual for $4.99 (one time purchase) or Milton Family for $14.99. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every week, I cast an eye over the latest arrivals on Prime Video, all in an effort to pick out the latest thrillers added to the streaming service library.

While November continues to be dominated by Christmas movies, I've still been able to find three worthwhile thrillers. Okay, so one is more of an action-horror, but it does have its share of thriller-style twists and turns. The other two are a psychological trip and an '80s classic starring Matthew "Ferris Bueller" Broderick. Each one is worthy of your streaming consideration.

So, let's jump into the three latest to Prime Video thriller movies I recommend you watch this week.

Perhaps the most “traditional” thriller among my picks this week, “Blink Twice” might not reinvent the genre, but it’s an intense watch that slowly builds tension until a shocking twist. It marked the directorial debut of Zoë Kravitz, and stars Naomi Ackie, most recently seen in “Clayface,” alongside Channing Tatum. It’s an effective first filmmaking effort from Kravitz, even if it’s perhaps not quite as intelligently plotted as the strong first act suggests.

Sources indicate that frida (Naomi Ackie) is a cocktail waitress at a swanky party where she meets tech tycoon Slater King (Channing Tatum). Invited to his private island for a vacation of unparalleled luxury, Frida and her friend Jess (Alia Shawkat) initially think they’ve found paradise, and Frida might have even found love with the charming tech mogul. But as lazy sun-soaked days blur into nights of glamorous partying, Frida can’t shake an uneasy feeling that something is wrong.

Watch "Blink Twice" on Prime Video now.

Industry observers note that three years before starring in one of the most popular movies of the 1980s, Matthew Broderick made his breakthrough with his second major feature film role. He might have made his debut in “Max Dugan Returns” in the spring of 1983. However, it was the techno-thriller “Wargames” released in the summer that saw Broderick identified as a talent to watch, and, well, those labeling him a rising star at the time were certainly proved right.

According to recent reports, sure, it’s a little outdated in the 21st century, but "Wargames" is still a compelling mix of technology-driven thrills and teen drama. David Lightman (Broderick) is a gifted high schooler but with a lazy streak. A computer whiz, he uses his aptitude for computers to unknowingly access a military central computer with the ability to simulate and even launch a devastating nuclear attack against the USSR. Unaware that he’s playing with real weapons of war and thinking he’s playing a video game, he might have ignited World War III.

Watch "Wargames" on Prime Video now.

Rounding out my picks this week is “They Will Kill You,” a real genre-blender that mixes action, horror, comedy, and thriller elements into a movie that isn’t exactly tonally consistent, but does have quite a few slick moments. Most notably, there's a very fiery action sequence and a satisfying early reveal that flips the storyline on its head. It’s also a great showcase for Zazie Beetz, who is best known for her TV roles in “Atlanta,” “Easy” and “Invincible.”.

It has been revealed that asia (Beetz) arrives at a posh Fresh York City high-rise apartment building posing as a maid, but she’s really hoping to find her missing sister. Once in the complex, she discovers it’s not just home to the city's wealthy and elite, but houses a satanic cult. I’ll say no more for fear of spoiling the surprises within this action-horror, but let’s say things get very bloody, very fast. “They Will Kill You” is stylish, taking cues from Quentin Tarantino, even if it never matches the iconic director’s sharp writing and memorable characters.

Watch "They Will Kill You" on Prime Video starting November 20.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • When you Googled something, you used to get a link to my website.
  • It has been revealed that it’s hard to fund my work with only a quarter of my audience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this is the traffic to All About Berlin, the website that I run since 2017, and live from since 2020. After 7 years of growth, it has lost 70% 75% of its traffic to Google AI Overviews.

When you Googled something, you used to get a link to my website. Now you get a page of ads, then an AI-generated answer trained on my content, then finally a link to my website. This has a devastating impact on traffic.

It has been revealed that it’s hard to fund my work with only a quarter of my audience. Soon, I will need another way to pay my rent. Instead of writing new guides, I already spend my days preparing for that future.

Industry observers note that it’s not just about the money. I have poured 8 years of my life into making something good and useful. Strangers’ faces light up when they learn that I run All About Berlin. Local and federal government offices refer people to my guides. The Berlin immigration office uses my data about themselves. It inspired two government portals and a few similar websites in other cities.

If my work just get mixed into an AI-generated answer, I lose my voice and my audience. My carefully chosen words lose their meaning. No one shakes my hand and buys me a beer. No one tells me how their citizenship application went.

This is not an isolated case. Many website owners have reached out in private to commiserate. Some have paywalled their work. Others have given up and moved on. They keep the websites online, but they no longer enhancement them. It’s just not worth it.

According to recent reports, it will get worse. Last week, Google has made two announcements: AI-generated answers will replace search results entirely, and they have ads in them.1 This is the future of the internet. No websites, just a chat box with ads.

I don’t know where All About Berlin fits in that future.

This was also discussed on Mastodon, Hacker News, LinkedIn and Twitter. If you are affected, reach out. Let me know how you are doing. You are not going through this alone.

10 Hacks Every watchOS 27 User Should Know

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1354 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that watchOS 27 introduces a solid set of upgrades to your wrist—assuming your Apple Watch supports it.
  • With watchOS 27, Apple changed what double-pressing the Digital Crown does.
  • It seems Apple realized the mistake, however, as evidenced by watchOS 27.2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that watchOS 27 introduces a solid set of upgrades to your wrist—assuming your Apple Watch supports it. While the newest update isn't Apple's most feature-filled, it does include a number of changes that improve the way you exercise, track your health, and locate missing items. That's especially true for anyone with the latest Series 12 or Ultra 4. If your Apple Watch supports watchOS 27, you should know about these 10 hacks:.

With watchOS 27, Apple changed what double-pressing the Digital Crown does. Instead of opening the app switcher, it now triggers Audio Intelligence—if you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. If you don't have access to those features, the gesture now does nothing.

It seems Apple realized the mistake, however, as evidenced by watchOS 27.2. When you're using an app while running this latest upgrade, press and hold the bottom part of the watch's screen, and you'll trigger the app switcher. You can now jump to a different app, or close an app that isn't working. Sadly, this only works when you're already in an app, and not when you're on the Home Screen, but it's certainly better than nothing.

It has been revealed that while you can load up multiple complications on your Apple Watch, they aren't exactly dynamic. That's why I'm a major fan of the Smart Stack widgets on the Apple Watch, which update dynamically to show contextual information. Now, with the new Siri Modular Face, you can access dynamic widgets on the Home Screen. If you've just parked your car, for example, you'll see a widget showing its location; likewise, if you have an upcoming calendar appointment, it will be front and center.

Sources indicate that to use the Siri Modular watch face, tap and hold on the screen, go to the end of the list, tap the Plus button, and find and add the Siri Modular watch face. Once you do, you'll start seeing dynamic widgets when you wake up your watch. Don't expect much personalization from this watch face, however. You can customize the colors and add three small complications, but that's it.

According to recent reports, the double-tap gesture is one of my favorite Apple Watch features. By tapping your thumb and index finger together twice, you can do things like answer a call or reply to a message. In watchOS 27, Apple took the gesture one step forward. You can now use the double-tap gesture to scroll through your widgets; if you perform a single tap, it then opens the highlighted widget or the shortcut. This means you can open and browse the weather app, or start a workout, without ever touching your Apple Watch's screen.

Your Apple Watch's fresh Music Recognition app has native Shazam integration. What's more, Shazam will record your request even when you're offline and away from your iPhone. The moment you reconnect, the service will identify the songs, which you can see in the Shazam app on your iPhone or Apple Watch.

In a recent development, it seems like Apple has a library of songs it uses for offline recognition, because in my testing, it was able to recognize a Coldplay song instantly, even when in Airplane mode. To use it, you can either open the Music Recognition app, or you can add the widget for faster access. Scroll up on the Home Screen, go to the bottom of the screen, tap the Edit button, then the Plus button, and add the Music Recognition widget.

Apple Watches have traditionally lacked a live step count widget or complication. To find your step count, you had to go to the bottom of the Activity app, or rely on third-party apps. But even still, these apps never showed live data. You’d always have to wait a couple of seconds to see the updated stats.

In a recent development, now, if you own the latest Apple Watch Series 12 or the Ultra 4, you can add a live step count widget or complication to the Apple Watch face or the Smart Stack. This will show you your precise step count at all times. To use it, go to the bottom of the Smart Stack, tap the Edit button, then tap the Plus button. Here, find and add the newly introduced Step count widget.

Siri is no longer a voice assistant that you use for one-off tasks. With Siri AI, you can now carry on multiple conversations with context and memory. It's not as robust as ChatGPT or Claude, but you can use Siri AI for brainstorming, researching, and jotting down ideas for later.

The Siri AI app on the iPhone shows all your conversations, and so does the Apple Watch. This means you can continue your Siri AI conversations and view past chats on your Apple Watch. To use it, press the Digital Crown once, then tap the Siri app icon in the center. This will open up all your conversations instead of calling upon Siri. Tap a conversation to continue your chat on the Apple Watch. Of course, anything you do here will be reflected in the Siri app on your iPhone.

The latest Find My app on the Apple Watch demonstrates a single map for finding people, devices, and items. This means you can now locate your family members who are sharing their location with you, as well as AirTags or other Find My items from the watchOS app.

It has been revealed that after opening the app, you can use the Digital Crown to zoom in or out of the map. Use touch to pan around. The map doesn't show all items and people at once, though. Tap the Menu button at the bottom-right corner, and then switch between People, Items, or Devices. If you have multiple items, you can scroll through them using the Digital Crown.

While it's not a Whoop-level feature, the Apple Watch now includes a Readiness score. Instead of individually looking at your training load, sleep score, and vitals, you now have one number that gives you the whole picture.

Sources indicate that the Readiness score ranges from 0 to 10 and is based on your recent fitness activity, sleep data, and background health monitoring. If you have a score of 8 to 10, your Apple Watch thinks you can push yourself, or "go for it," as it says; if it's below 5, the watch thinks you should consider lighter activity. This feature, though, is only available on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. You can use the upcoming Readiness app on your Apple Watch to see this data, but you can also access it on your iPhone in the Fitness app's new Readiness section.

Recent findings suggest that low Power Mode isn't your only option when it comes to extending the battery life for your Apple Watch. watchOS 27 offers a special Max Extended Workout mode just for long workouts. With it, your Apple Watch disables some features, like splits and alerts, and reduces the frequency of GPS and heart rate readings, in the hopes of extending your battery throughout your entire exercise. To use it, go to the Workout app and select the workout you want. Tap the Goals button in the top-right corner, and choose the Extended option. Then, switch to the Max Extended option and start your workout.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 come with a set of Audio Intelligence features that use the microphones on the Apple Watch, paired with AI models (both local and cloud-based), to identify sounds, music, and record conversation. Thanks to this fresh feature, one of the iPhone's accessibility features also makes its way to the Apple Watch.

Sources indicate that sound Recognition can alert you when it hears sirens, alarms, doorbells, and more, even when your iPhone isn’t around. To set this up, go to the Settings app on your iPhone and navigate to Accessibility > Sound & Name Recognition > Sound Recognition. Here, enable the sounds you want to monitor, and make sure to turn on the Detect using Apple Watch toggle.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In September, Apple introduced the new Beats 360 headphones, the first overears from Beats since the Beats Studio Pro in 2023. That mentioned, the older Beats Studio Pro still remain on sale at a lower price point – so it begs the question, which Beats headphones are more worthwhile?

One of the biggest differences between the two will be the price. The Beats Studio Pro, since they’re older, are regularly available on discount. At the moment, you can pick up Beats Studio Pro for $199-249 on Amazon, compared to Beats 360, which aren’t discounted from their $349 launch pricing.

Despite being older and cheaper, the Beats Studio Pro have a couple advantages over the Beats 360. On top of the fact that they’re $100-150 cheaper, you may very well still want to consider them.

The biggest advantages, in my view, have to do with the form factor. The Beats Studio Pro can fold down into a much more compact size, whereas Beats 360 don’t fold at all. This means it’s easier to carry around the Beats Studio Pro.

Beats Studio Pro also offer a headphone jack, whereas Beats 360 don’t have any sort of wired audio at all, even over USB-C. This means Beats Studio Pro are easier to use in environments where bluetooth audio isn’t convenient, such as with a game console or on an airplane.

One of my favorite things about the Beats 360 is that they offer UltraPlush cushions you can swap into, but those cost extra. Beats Studio Pro by default come with UltraPlush cushions, so you can have a more comfortable experience out of the box.

Of course, Beats 360 are newer, so by default they do a number of things better. That includes:.

Industry observers note that out of everything on this list, I’d say clearer transparency, stronger noise cancellation, and automatic device switching make the biggest difference. In my testing, its hard to hear with the transparency mode on the Beats Studio Pro, so I end up taking the headphones off to have conversation. With Beats 360, that isn’t the case.

As for noise cancellation and automatic device switching, I feel that if you’re buying Beats for the sake of having Apple headphones, you should buy the ones that offer true automatic device switching – and those are the Beats 360. Noise cancellation is more of a personal preference, but if you value having the best noise cancellation, the Beats 360 are noticeably better.

It has been revealed that lastly, the Beats 360 do have the customizable design going for them. While customization is more aesthetically pleasing, it also has an advantage longer term – when the earcups start wearing down over the years, you can swiftly replace them on the Beats 360.

Recent findings suggest that while it’s hard to overlook the fact that Beats Studio Pro come in at a much lower price point, I’d generally say that if you want a great pair of headphones that offer an Apple experience, you probably shouldn’t buy the Beats Studio Pro. The Beats Studio Pro are a fine pair of headphones for the price, but you certainly aren’t getting all of the same ecosystem creature comforts that Beats 360 offer.

That noted, Beats 360 simply do not offer a headphone jack or a foldable design, and if those things matter to you, then Beats Studio Pro might still be the way to go. Beats Studio Pro also offer a ton of different color options that aren’t available on Beats 360, while costing $150 less.
