Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Complexdiscovery

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s Note: Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, yet finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, according to a working paper by Harvard Ph.D.
  • According to recent reports, for eDiscovery, privacy and compliance professionals, the study suggests a measurement approach for legal AI buyers: consider approved work product, revision rates and reviewer time alongside drafting output.
  • A short percentage-based assessment of the qualitative benefit expressed as a percentage of positive reception of the recent article from ComplexDiscovery OÜ titled, "Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note: Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, yet finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, according to a working paper by Harvard Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton covering 718 firms. The paper, a job-market paper with no indication of completed peer review, measures what happens at the human checkpoint once drafting speeds up. Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and Cooley’s redaction agent, still in development with Google Cloud, both keep a lawyer at a comparable checkpoint, and neither announcement reports a measure of that review stage.

According to recent reports, for eDiscovery, privacy and compliance professionals, the study suggests a measurement approach for legal AI buyers: consider approved work product, revision rates and reviewer time alongside drafting output. It also reveals that AI authorship can leave metadata in collaboration systems that records and legal hold programs may need to reach. Watch for a revised version of the paper and for any legal vendor that publishes review-stage figures, keeping in mind that the study examined software, not legal work.

A short percentage-based assessment of the qualitative benefit expressed as a percentage of positive reception of the recent article from ComplexDiscovery OÜ titled, "Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review.".

News Analysis – Artificial Intelligence Beat.

Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, but finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, a Harvard working paper found.

Sources indicate that in the study’s data, the extra coding produced no detectable rise in finished work, and code review became the bottleneck. Fiona Chen and James Stratton, both Ph.D. candidates at Harvard University, measured that pattern across 725,938 workers at 718 companies. Two legal AI announcements this month, Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and a court-filing redaction agent Cooley is developing with Google Cloud, place a lawyer at a comparable review step, and neither reports a measure of it.

How much weight that pattern can bear depends on where the numbers came from. Chen and Stratton built the study on data from Jellyfish, a organization that sells an analytics platform tracking engineering activity, and joined it to LinkedIn employment records collected by Revelio Labs. The sample runs from January 2021 to March 2026 and covers Jellyfish client firms that consented to research use of their data. The paper’s tables list 68.3 million Jira concerns, 200.9 million commits, 49.1 million pull requests and 21.3 million calendar events, though only 213 of the 718 firms supplied calendar data.

Sources indicate that the design is a staggered difference-in-differences comparison, which tracks month by month how outcomes changed at adopting firms against firms that had not yet adopted. A comparison like that is only as good as the reasons adoption dates differed, and here the authors point to a process legal and security teams will recognize, because they sit inside it. The paper says timing was shaped mainly by when firms learned about the tools and by how long procurement took, meaning sourcing, legal and security approvals and pilot programs. One interviewee’s firm approved a tool in about a day; another interviewee put the average approval time at six to 12 months.

In a recent development, the authors call those procurement delays plausibly unrelated to how fast a firm was growing, which they argue supports comparing early and late adopters. They acknowledge one known imbalance, that larger firms adopted earlier, and they control for firm size. If some hidden difference remains, the authors say, it would more likely make AI look more productive than it is, not less. A bias in that direction would make the flat output result, if anything, generous to AI.

Sources indicate that the current version of the paper is dated Aug. 4, 2026, and the first was dated Jan. 7. Chen circulated it as her job-market paper, and nothing in the version reviewed for this article indicates journal acceptance or completed peer review. Her website lists coverage links to The Wall Street Journal and The Economist, and legal trade press picked it up this month, including an Oct. 12 eDiscovery Today post by Doug Austin that relayed an Ars Technica report.

With that provenance in view, the coding results are large. Lines of code added rose by 1,494 per worker-month against a baseline of 5,017, about 30 percent. Commits rose 20 percent, and pull requests, the bundles of code submitted for review, rose 23 percent. The authors note that these estimates capture the added effect of agents at firms that already had AI coding assistants, not the effect of AI from a standing start.

It has been revealed that output is where the gain stops. The paper counts finished work as Jira challenges resolved, and an issue counts as complete when its code is deployed to production. Agents moved that measure by 0.12 issues per worker-month on a 3.67 baseline, with a standard error of 0.17. That result is statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the 95 percent confidence interval rules out an increase above about 12 percent of the baseline, well short of the 30 percent rise in code written.

The authors tested the obvious escape route. If engineers had shifted to larger tasks, a flat problem count would understate real output. So the researchers labeled a 0.5 percent sample of concerns by size with GPT-4o and extended those labels to every issue with a text-embedding model. They found no shift in average issue size, and pull requests did not grow larger either, which the authors use to set aside the simplest explanation for what happened in review.

Sources indicate that the paper locates the shortfall in code review. The time from pull request submission to merge rose 3.45 days on a 7.03-day baseline, a 49 percent increase. The share of pull requests receiving a formal change request increased by about 12 percentage points from a baseline of 13 percent, nearly doubling, and review comments per pull request rose 35 percent. The share of workers doing any code review rose 14 percent from a base of about 29 percent, while the share writing code demonstrated no measurable change.

AI review tools did not remove the bottleneck. By March 2026, nearly 80 percent of the firms had used one, yet AI generated only 23.3 percent of review comments, and only 10.8 percent of pull requests received even one AI comment. The authors write that the bottleneck persists after firms adopt such tools. The paper’s interviews show what that looks like on a team: a junior software engineer described a project where only one senior engineer could approve changes and could review the interviewee’s code only once a week. “After some outages that were caused by AI-generated commits, there were also latest rules requiring senior engineer approval for AI-generated code, which created even more review bottlenecks,” the engineer mentioned, in a quote the authors say they lightly edited for clarity.

That account fits the model the authors use to explain their numbers, which has two channels. In the first, faster drafting sends more code to a fixed pool of reviewers, a problem that moving labor into review can largely relieve. In the second, the rise in change requests and comments, which faster drafting alone does not explain, reads through the model as a sign of lower-quality drafts. That problem, the authors say, would require better technology. Anyone buying an agent should care which channel dominates, because the two call for different spending.

Nor did the coding gains show up as job cuts. The estimates rule out a decline in overall employment larger than 2.9 percent. A noisier estimate rules out a decline in engineering employment larger than 13.8 percent. The authors caution that these are short-run effects measured in partial equilibrium, which could mask job losses at competing firms, and that the assistant estimate for engineering employment reveals upward pre-trends that make it hard to read causally.

Those software results arrive as legal AI tools adopt a related design, and the Harvey and Cooley announcements both follow it: automate a first pass, then keep a lawyer at the checkpoint. Harvey’s workflow, co-developed with LexisNexis and announced Oct. 7, is the drafting case. Harvey states the multi-step process of reading the complaint, researching and drafting a motion to dismiss “commonly takes 40 to 50+ hours of work” and that its tool produces the research and a first draft “in a matter of hours.” The announcement describes “human checkpoints at the moments where a lawyer’s judgment matters most,” but it does not state how long lawyers spend at those checkpoints or how long it takes to reach a motion ready to file.

Industry observers note that cooley’s Oct. 8 announcement applies the same posture to a different task, since its agent recommends redactions rather than drafting arguments. Cooley says the agent is still being developed and that attorneys make all redaction determinations before a filing goes to the court, which puts the human checkpoint at the last step before submission. As ComplexDiscovery reported Oct. 10, the announcement carries no error rate.

For a motion filed in federal court, the checkpoint is a legal duty rather than a design choice. Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b), an attorney presenting a motion certifies several things about it to the best of the attorney’s knowledge, information and belief, “formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances.” Its legal contentions must be “warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for extending, modifying, or reversing existing law or for establishing new law.” Its factual contentions must have evidentiary support or, if specifically so identified, be likely to have it after a reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery. A first draft can arrive in hours, but that inquiry stays with the attorney, and the software evidence raises the possibility that review could absorb some of the drafting savings.

The paper’s method carries a second lesson, this one for information governance teams. The researchers identified agent use partly from traces inside the firms’ own systems, including bot accounts tied to AI tools and signatures such as “Co-authored-by” lines in commit messages and pull request descriptions. AI authorship can leave its own metadata trail in collaboration systems. That trail is a record that a retention schedule and a legal hold may need to reach.

None of this means legal work will behave like software, and the limits of the comparison matter. Document review is not code review, a production is not a pull request, and Chen and Stratton studied no legal work. A separate National Bureau of Economic Research working paper, revised in September 2026, reports a similar falloff using data on over 500,000 GitHub developers. Its authors, Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff and Liyuan Yang, found a 240 percent cumulative rise in commits from autonomous agents shrinking to 30 percent for actual releases. That paper carries its own disclosure: Demirer and Musolff each previously held a postdoctoral research position at Microsoft, which owns GitHub, and each now works as a paid research consultant for the tech giant. Two software studies point to a pattern in software, not a finding about law firms.

Recent findings suggest that discovery practitioners have argued a version of this question before, and Austin’s post draws that comparison. He wrote that discovery has seen a similar debate over generative AI review, with some practitioners saying manual validation offsets the gains and others, including him, saying statistical sampling of the kind used in predictive coding is enough. For coding agents, though, he wrote that the extra review time may be warranted, since code that is 90 percent correct can still fail to run.

His comparison suggests a useful split between two kinds of legal output. Population-level work such as first-pass relevance review can be validated by sampling. A single filing is different, because its citations, factual assertions and sensitive data generally need direct examination when one fabricated citation or one missed Social Security number is the failure. Buyers can turn that split into a test. Ask a vendor which kind of output its agent produces, then ask for the downstream measure rather than the drafting one: hours from upload to an approved work product, the share of drafts a reviewing attorney sent back and reviewer time per matter. Budget review capacity before scaling drafting volume, and log what reviewers change, because that log reveals whether the bottleneck is volume or quality.

Those questions apply to the paper’s own sourcing, too. The data partner has a commercial interest in the subject, and the relationship runs deeper than a data license. Jellyfish describes itself as an “AI Impact Platform,” and the authors have published on its blog: a Sept. 25, 2025, post by Chen and Stratton described itself as “part of our ongoing work with Jellyfish.” The paper thanks the Jellyfish team “for their partnership” and states that Jellyfish reviewed the manuscript only to check for proprietary disclosure, not for scientific content, and that the conclusions are the authors’. Its funders were the Stripe Economics of AI Fellowship, a Harvard Kennedy School program on wealth distribution and the Schmidt Sciences AI at Work Program.

Recent findings suggest that jellyfish has also promoted an earlier version of the work. A Jan. 28 post on its blog by Nicholas Arcolano called it “a preliminary version of a newly introduced paper from our collaborators at Harvard Economics, Fiona Chen and James Stratton,” based on 100,000 software engineers across 500 companies. That post, and a March 17 Jellyfish press release after it, reported that AI was making coding faster and that “code quality doesn’t seem to be suffering.” The August version, built on a larger sample running through March 2026, reads the near-doubling in change requests through its model as a possible sign of lower draft quality. The two descriptions rest on different versions and samples, so they need not conflict, but a reader relying on Jellyfish’s summary would miss the quality question the current paper raises.

In a recent development, the paper also carries small internal inconsistencies that do not touch the headline agent estimates. Its introduction rounds the sample to about 700 firms and 700,000 workers, and its main text describes 17 interviews where an appendix describes 21. Other limits are structural rather than clerical: the underlying data are proprietary, and use of AI tools through individual licenses goes unrecorded.

Recent findings suggest that none of those caveats overturns the central result, though the March 2026 data cutoff means a revision could move the figures. What the paper offers is a standard the two legal announcements discussed here do not meet: named authors, a disclosed method, a confidence interval and a measured checkpoint. If an agent cuts 40 hours of research and drafting to a few, how many of those hours reappear on the desk of the lawyer who signs the motion?

iOS 27.3 beta 2 is now available, and Apple is adding the ability for users to unlock higher usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI via iCloud+. Here’s everything you need to know.

From the start, Apple has mentioned that some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features have usage limits because “they rely on powerful server models.” The tech giant previously outlined that increased access would be available across most iCloud+ subscription aims, and now we have the full details on how this will work.

Apple says the newly introduced system applies to several categories of Apple Intelligence features, including:.

The usage limits are per device, not per account. This means your iPhone, iPad, and Mac each have separate allowances. Apple isn’t disclosing specific limit numbers. Instead, it indicates that limits can vary based on the feature, request complexity, system demand, and more.

In a recent development, as you near your limit, you’ll see an alert within whichever feature you’re using. For example, if you are using Image Playground, a message will appear telling you that you’ve almost hit your usage limit for the day. Once you hit the limit, you’ll be prompted to wait for it to reset or upgrade your iCloud+ initiative.

If you hit your limit, basic Siri requests will still work. This includes things like setting timers and alarms. Requests that require Siri to understand personal context and perform more complex, multi-step actions, however, are subject to the limits.

For example, asking Siri to find the details of an upcoming dinner reservation in your email and add them to your calendar would count toward your daily limit.

It has been revealed that additionally, each device uses its own standard daily usage limit first. After that, it can tap into the additional capacity included with an eligible iCloud+ subscription:.

Sources indicate that the usage unlocked by iCloud+ is shared across all devices signed in to your Apple Account, as well as family members sharing your iCloud+ strategy. The shared usage is available on a first-come, first-served basis.

Sources indicate that all limits will reset daily at the same time, and limits don’t roll over. In most cases, limits reset around midnight in your current time zone.

Apple has published a support document with more details.

macOS 27.3 includes newly introduced privacy controls for Full Disk Access and more

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (616 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last month, Apple confirmed its plans to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access amid the rise of “increasingly capable and autonomous” AI agents.
  • With today’s new macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this.
  • In a post on its developer website last month, Apple said some developers are “using Full Disk Access in ways that could put customers at risk, exposing everything on their systems.” As such, it said that it would “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last month, Apple confirmed its plans to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access amid the rise of “increasingly capable and autonomous” AI agents.

With today’s new macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this.

In a post on its developer website last month, Apple said some developers are “using Full Disk Access in ways that could put customers at risk, exposing everything on their systems.” As such, it said that it would “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”.

In macOS 27.2, “Device Control and Data Access” is a unified toggle in System Settings, where Apple says that apps with that level of access can “view and send email, edit contacts and photos, monitor your keyboard, track websites, record your screen, control any app on your Mac, and more.”.

In macOS 27.3, Apple is splitting “Device Control and Data Access” into two categories:.

Sources indicate that for the latter, users will be able to specify which apps an automation tool can access rather than granting it unrestricted control. For instance, you could give an app access to the Mail app, but not Messages.

macOS 27.3 also adds an option for users to require an app to request permission every time it needs access, rather than granting it access indefinitely.

Apple is also introducing a upcoming menu bar indicator that will provide additional transparency when an app is controlling another app with System and App Protection Override. This is designed to let owners know when an automation tool is interacting with apps and information in the background.

Crucially, Apple isn’t removing the ability to give an app Full Disk Access. If you deem it necessary, you can still give an app Full Disk Access. However, Apple is redesigning the approval process to make the implications of that decision more obvious.

macOS 27.3 will display a more detailed explanation about the protections being bypassed and the types of personal information that could be exposed.

Industry observers note that users can also choose to grant an app access to specific folders instead of their entire Mac. For example, an app that only needs to work with files in a particular folder won’t get unrestricted access to everything else.

Any app you’ve already given Full Disk Access will still have that access. Previously granted permissions will remain in effect, and those apps will continue functioning as they do today without any approval required.

Apple has published a new support document detailing the Full Disk Access updates.

It has been revealed that macOS 27.3 now warns you before giving an app full disk accessThat warning prompt is pretty scary! pic.twitter.com/J2qCKVWJRx.

Apple claims the underlying APIs aren’t changing, but developers will need to upgrade their apps to account for situations where users grant limited access rather than unrestricted permissions.

Finally, Apple indicates developers of backup apps and assistive technologies can request entitlements that allow them to maintain the same experience for upcoming installations as before macOS 27.3. Apple has already identified popular apps that rely on these permissions, and those apps will continue working as expected without requiring an entitlement.

Developers can read more on Apple’s Developer website.

#27674. Breaking: Dissecting Spring petclinic (Part 2 – Bending the persistence)

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 32m • 📚 Deep Dive (6313 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Github ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Dissecting Spring petclinic (Part 2 – Bending the persistence)

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 32 min read (6313 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~32 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is the second entry in a series of blog posts about Spring.
  • This is the second entry in a series of blog posts about Spring.
  • This time, I replaced Spring data with JDBI, close to pure SQL and some simple POJOs to represent persisted data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the second entry in a series of blog posts about Spring. Make sure to read my entry post and previous entries before this one. This time, I replaced Spring data with JDBI, close to pure SQL and some simple POJOs to represent persisted data TLDR Spring data and Hibernate (or JPA as well) do a lot of necessary work for you. It's really great when you are okay with its requirements. Staying pure, simple and data-centric when it comes to persistence is not as easy as one thinks, at least not for applications that need a lot of data creation I don't think I changed the project for the better with my latest changes. I can only see them as a necessary step towards the greater goal. How it started When I explored the petclinic project, I realized that in most of the tests, I didn't immediately have an idea what exactly is tested. I tackled this problem with the stuff I wrote about in Part 1 of the series. I also realized, that I don't consider the existing tests to be particularly good for a set of reasons. Even though I enhanced a few of those concerns, some are still left in there. For example a good test should make clear what data is arranged, what functionality is triggered and what behaviour is expected. The arrangement of the data is ideally done right in the test to keep locality of reasoning high and to have tests being independent of each other. Let's take a look at an existing test. Here you can find the OwnerControllerTest. There is a test @Test void testShowOwner() throws Exception { var httpResponse = get("http://localhost:" + port + "/owners/" + TEST_OWNER_ID); assertEquals(200, httpResponse.statusCode()); assertThat(httpResponse.body().toString()).containsSubsequence("","","Name","","","","George Franklin", ... assertThat(httpResponse.body().toString()).containsSubsequence("","","","Visit Date","","","Description","","","","","","2024-10-10", .... } Let's ignore for a second that the actual assertions (that I wrote, not the petclinic authors) could be more speaking and concise. Why should the get request in this test lead to George Franklin being present on the owners page? We can try to find out what this "TEST_OWNER_ID" is that is referenced. But it will only lead us to a top level declaration without any further info. What happened is, that I worsened the code in this class, because before, there was some class scoped init code before, that actually made explicit what data was initialized before each test. On the upside, I removed a lot of boilerplate. Well. Since I had something like this in my mind when I applied the first changes to the project, I converted all the tests to use a real database - and then, i realized that there was actually a set of default data already present in an sql file. This is one of those magic, unexplorable things Spring does for you. You can not find the answer to why this data is created for the test in the test anywhere. Here's a good read about the topic, how to explicitly override it etc. pp, but the point stands: a feature that favours convenience over actual readability and explorability. NOTE: This statement is not unique to Spring, a lot of tools have a mechanism like that, some name the file a bit different or place it in a different location. This is not only a common critique towards Spring Data in particular, but it's also something I stumbled over in a lot of Spring projects: By default, most of them start off using Spring Data. Then again, most of them kept it, if not all of them. Then, all of them made me and my colleagues struggle again and again with the implicitness of how the data looks like, how it is organized, how it is accessed. In a lot of projects, we had to get creative in order to solve the eager/lazy loading glitch when entities reference each other. So let's see if we have just "skill issue" here and find out whether there could be a simpler approach at all. Let's remove Spring data completely and replace it with some very simple mapping library like JDBI. How it went Now, to get closer to what I consider the ideal solution in those tests, I need to get some aspects of the old code back - the local repository reference and the ability to add things to it and clear it. Since the goal is to replace the existing implementations, this is where I added an interface layer and created repository classes for all existing entity types that are independent of Spring (well, almost, the PageableImpl class is handy). Deactivating the default implementations A first gotcha is something that would be very simple with good old code: How to disable the existing persistence completely and switch to the upcoming, in-memory implementation? It could be val ownerRepository = InMemoryRepository() instead of val ownerRepository = SpringDataOwnerRepository(). But the latter doesn't exist. We only have an interface, while the implementation is created by the container, out of our control. Here you have a stackoverflow post with a wall of text that can now be remarked to this seemingly simple change of the project. Now, when the real implementation is deactivated, the tests will complain that a bean definition can't be found, so we have to provide the new implementations somehow. Here's the next wall of text what could be said to the topic when Spring comes into play - I wil just refer to the single line of code a few lines above what the ideal solution could look like. Furthermore. There is something that is a helper to launch an application in combination with a databse locally without much hassle, just a main method: MysqlTestApplication.java. It's in the test sources so that Testcontainers can be used to run the database. When I override the beans, right in this @Configuration-annotated class, then those definitions affect the whole rest of the source set - for example I tried to just disable the Spring data stuff and define my in-memory implementations with @Bean declarations and suddenly my OwnerControllerTest failed with a duplicate bean definition error. Yes, I know why this happens technically. But it's just another example of needless entanglement of things that should naturally just work completely independent. Again, let's compare it to the vanilla version in terms of simplicity and robustness. Let's continue. I would like to move this @TestConfiguration with my new repositories into the super class, so that all tests can simply reuse them and so that I can abstract over that stuff a bit to counter Java's verbosity. And then of course I can also inject the repositories so that all tests can just freely use them. Boom. Unsatisfied dependency error at runtime. Okay okay, then I will move the field declarations into the test, we make a compromise. Boom. Doesn't work. Okay, okay, I will create a seperate class, then use @Import on the base test and then I can finally inject the stuff in the base test. Phew. The next thing that somewhat surprised me is the duplication of the dummy data initialization. I would have expected those simple things to just use core sql and then apply the same script to all database implementations. But not the case, there were three different implementations. This might very well be for demonstration purposes, as the petclinic supports multiple database implemenations, like Postgres or MySQL, I haven't tried to unify it yet. Records: the disappointment I was looking forward to removing the entity classes code bloat alltogehter and replace them with Java records. This is not possible, because records are immutable and entities need to be mutable, otherwise they won't work with jpa or the whole model bindings for the views. I mean I knew that, but I ran into it again nonetheless. I continued to go in that direciton by at least using records for the new queries I replaced the entities with, but it turned out to be just aweful because of all the mapping and conversion bloat. At the given point, I can't convert eveything to be data-centric, rather than state-centric. Maybe at some later iteration. In comparison with Kotlin's data classes, records have really bad ergonomics, I have to state. And I am surprised what an effect worse usability of a vital thing like data modeling has on (my) coding. Actually removing entities As written above, I didn't replace the old entity classes. But I managed to remove all JPA annotations and made them POJOs. This was actually super hard, because the whole project relied on their structure. One view had a list of owners, each with a list of pets, each with a list of vet visits. When removing the list of viits from a pet, the view will simply receive null values, no static typing with thymeleaf. Those cases had to be replaced with multiple parameters in the model and for example a map that can be indexed by owner or respectively pet id. Switch to JDBI Besides those connection concerns I mentioned above, switching to JDBI was more or less straight-forward. We can easily reuse the existing datasource that Spring injects into the new database class and instantiate a JDBI instance from it. In tests, everything works fine, but for regular setup, I get connection refused errors wich I am not able to track down. Nothing seems to help. The biggest effort however, was in translating hibernate query language to sql. I would have loved to keep hibernate query language as it gives us platform independence and convenience, something that I worsened by converting to sql. But unfortunately, hibernate strictly relies on using entities and explicitly not just database tables directly. I would wish for using hibernate query language without the entity layer, but I guess it's not possible. By the way, the Hibernate documentation is excellent, a really recommended read. The conversion demonstrated me, how much stuff JPA, Hibernate or even Spring data do for you behind the scenes. I won't say it's the best way how they do it, but at least partly it's necessary stuff that you need to do by hand as well. For example an upsert - have you ever done that with pure SQL? There'slot of stuff to know about that. For example when you have some owner data. With JPA your entity is always connected to the database context and you can query it, save your data to a row by calling a simple method and it just saves the stuff for you whether it's new or not. Without such a tool, you have a lot of options, for example first you could execute a statement to find out if a row with a given id exists. or you could do an update statement and take a look how many rows are affected and only if none were execute an insert statement. And then you need to be careful which database implementations can give you back data as result and how it is actually returned - in one case I got a BigInteger back instead of an Int, for a generated id - maybe it could be a Long as well, who knows all that? And you will only find out at runtime, when you run with that actual database implementation. Additionally, I had to duplicate property lists because I needed those two statements for every table where I wanted to do an upsert. Not pretty and prone to errors when you forget to add a new property to your data/column to your tables. Take a look at what bloat I created for upserting - it was a simple owner.save() before: public Owner save(Owner owner) { jdbi.inTransaction(handle -> { var updatedRowsCount = owner.getId() == null ? 0 : handle.createUpdate(""" update owners set first_name = :firstName, last_name = :lastName, address = :address, city = :city, telephone = :telephone where id = :id RETURNING * """) .bindBean(owner) .execute(); if(updatedRowsCount == 0) { Map id = handle.createUpdate(""" insert into owners (first_name, last_name, address, city, telephone) values (:firstName, :lastName, :address, :city, :telephone) """) .bindBean(owner) .executeAndReturnGeneratedKeys("id") .mapToMap().one(); var idObject = id.values().stream().findFirst().get(); if (idObject instanceof BigInteger) { owner.setId(((BigInteger) idObject).intValue()); } else if (idObject instanceof Integer) { owner.setId((Integer) idObject); } else if (idObject instanceof Long) { owner.setId(((Long) idObject).intValue()); } else { throw new IllegalStateException("Don't understand id value: " + idObject); } } return null; }); return owner; } All in all, I don't think I did any good to the actual queries - I think they were better before. The good thing is, that by implementing all data handling it got explicit, so there's no question anymore where what is fetched or not. It's simply written out and you can debug into it. Schema handling in general I saw, that there is schema generation functionality in Hibernate, which can generate your db schema from your entities. Well, I want to state that I think this is exactly the opposite way it should be done: I strongly believe that the persistence - which is a boundary between now and the past that you have no chance to remove - should be the dominating element in this relationship. I consider the approach taken by JOOQ or SqlDelight the best one: Define the schema natively. Including migrations, they are inevitable. Then derive your types from there. SqlDelight does this just perfectly. So I am looking forward to applying that conversion at some point in the petclinic project. Spring, why you so slow Not exactly related to the persistence topic, but I have to get it off my chest: Everything in this project takes so much time, it's annoying. When executing tests in the ide the standard way, the task processTestAot takes 3-4 seconds of time. Every. Single. Time. Maybe there's a way to skip it, maybe it can be simply excluded by adding -x to the gradle config, or the gradle default config, so that it's also applied to every new run config that is created when I run a single test - but tbh I don't care. Another 1,5 - 2 seconds is spent setting up the docker client and starting the db container - this is likely my fault, because I made every test use a true database. I will eventually remove that, as soon as I removed Spring and the static test annotations, so that I can easily abstract over starting a container or not. From the first rendering of the petclinic logo on the command line to the first failing/succeeding test, it takes 22 whopping seconds. The test execution itself is in ms. This got just way out of hand - whatever the reason is that stuff is so slow. Usually people now start to tell me that stuff should be unit tested and mocked and Spring's sliced contexts should be used and then everything will be faster, yada yada yada. No. This is the benchmark. If worsening the way of working (imo) and making the actual code worse (imo) just to please the framework that is dominating you, than that's just plain bad. In the professional Spring projects (and other techstack as well), there are usually always a bunch of people knowing more details about the framework in use and usually do some magic tweaks here and there and do some education why strange feature xy should be used in order to improve self-imposed issue xyz and so on. At the current point in my carrer, I dislike that. I see increasing complexity because it's additional info you have to process, handle, update, keep and pass. The onboarding increases. The damage of "uneducated" people increases, because more people don't know enough to be "stellar" in that area. I always think that there is a different way to do things, it's just that we need to want it, actually. Curious if I will regret my current point of view in the future, but doesn't look like it, so far. Converting sql dummy data to code I was a bit puzzled when I saw the amount of sql code, for example for the example data. When I moved all tests to use real databases, I somehow needed needed to have data setup in every test, whereever it was needed. This was not possible with the old interfaces and so I just stick to using (and slightly adjusting...) the example data, so that I can test with that. I now exchanged that with fine granular data initialization per test, so that each test now has it's arragent-act-assert structure better recognizable. Here's an example. // In base class, applied to every test subclass @BeforeEach void beforeEach() { database.clear(); } // In base class, used by a lot of tests public @NotNull Owner createGeorge() { var george = createOwner("George", "Franklin", "110 W. Liberty St.", "Madison", "6085551023"); var milo = createPet(george.getId(), "Milo", database.findPetTypes().get(0)); var visit = createVisit(milo.getId(), LocalDate.of(2023, 10, 2)); return george; } // In some actual test @Test void testInitUpdateOwnerForm() throws Exception { var george = createGeorge(); var httpResponse = get("http://localhost:" + port + "/owners/" + george.getId() + "/edit"); assertEquals(200, httpResponse.statusCode()); assertTrue(httpResponse.body().toString().contains("")); [...] } So all in all, there was some short amount of time where I misused the example sql files to setup test data. That didn't then work with the in-memory implementation of the database/repository interfaces and I would have needed to convert it to create the test data programmatically. That's normally what I prefer, because it's reusable then and doesn't need to get duplicated per database. Once again, I miss Kotlin's features like default values, named parameters and data classes - with Java, I needed to have some ugly factory methods and I am not able to easily override parts of the data for some specific tests. I also won't go down the rabbit hole of creating a lot of builder pattern boilperplate for that, it's too much noise for what is aimed to achieve. Closing words Here's the commit containing all the changes connected to this blog post. I underestimated the effort and knowledge that is needed to replace JPA or similar from a project like petclinic. I created unnecessary effort by not focusing on the best way to approach the problem, or generally the best way of doing anything in life: By doing tiniest possbile steps, get to a safepoint and work with the gained experience. I tried to replace exiting entities with records and created code bloat that didn't work out. I was too stubborn to accept it early and wasted too much time on it. My biggest insight in this iteration was how much fun it can be to dissect the flow of data through an application. How is data connected, where is it fetched, what are the states that need to be handled? Whenever I thought I understood a piece of code, I rewrote its data usage to what I would have liked it to look. Objectively though, I don't think I made much - if anything - better in this project with this iteration. Just a bit different. And I also have the feeling I just added some errors or made some mistakes here and there. I personally still prefer explicitness and the close-to-the-core-language aspect of a tool like JDBI, but I can also definetely see the value of frameworks like JPA, Spring data and especially Hibernate. I wonder whether using Hibernate without joined entities is the best way to do persistence, because it would give you the simplicity of pure SQL approaches and simple mappers, but still prevents you from having to deal with the ugly bits of entities and any performance concerns. And it gives you Hibernate Query language <3. Up to the next big change in the petclinic. Maybe it will be switching the template engine - I can't say that I am enjoying Thymeleaf much :).

This is the second entry in a series of blog posts about Spring. Make sure to read my entry post and previous entries before this one.

This time, I replaced Spring data with JDBI, close to pure SQL and some simple POJOs to represent persisted data.

In a recent development, when I explored the petclinic project, I realized that in most of the tests, I didn't immediately have an idea what exactly is tested. I tackled this problem with the stuff I wrote about in Part 1 of the series. I also realized, that I don't consider the existing tests to be particularly good for a set of reasons. Even though I enhanced a few of those concerns, some are still left in there. For example a good test should make clear what data is arranged, what functionality is triggered and what behaviour is expected. The arrangement of the data is ideally done right in the test to keep locality of reasoning high and to have tests being independent of each other. Let's take a look at an existing test.

Here you can find the OwnerControllerTest. There is a test.

Let's ignore for a second that the actual assertions (that I wrote, not the petclinic authors) could be more speaking and concise. Why should the get request in this test lead to George Franklin being present on the owners page? We can try to find out what this "TEST_OWNER_ID" is that is referenced. But it will only lead us to a top level declaration without any further info. What happened is, that I worsened the code in this class, because before, there was some class scoped init code before, that actually made explicit what data was initialized before each test. On the upside, I removed a lot of boilerplate. Well. Since I had something like this in my mind when I applied the first changes to the project, I converted all the tests to use a real database - and then, i realized that there was actually a set of default data already present in an sql file. This is one of those magic, unexplorable things Spring does for you. You can not find the answer to why this data is created for the test in the test anywhere. Here's a good read about the topic, how to explicitly override it etc. pp, but the point stands: a feature that favours convenience over actual readability and explorability.

NOTE: This statement is not unique to Spring, a lot of tools have a mechanism like that, some name the file a bit different or place it in a different location.

This is not only a common critique towards Spring Data in particular, but it's also something I stumbled over in a lot of Spring projects: By default, most of them start off using Spring Data. Then again, most of them kept it, if not all of them. Then, all of them made me and my colleagues struggle again and again with the implicitness of how the data looks like, how it is organized, how it is accessed. In a lot of projects, we had to get creative in order to solve the eager/lazy loading issue when entities reference each other.

So let's see if we have just "skill issue" here and find out whether there could be a simpler approach at all. Let's remove Spring data completely and replace it with some very simple mapping library like JDBI.

In a recent development, now, to get closer to what I consider the ideal solution in those tests, I need to get some aspects of the old code back - the local repository reference and the ability to add things to it and clear it. Since the goal is to replace the existing implementations, this is where I added an interface layer and created repository classes for all existing entity types that are independent of Spring (well, almost, the PageableImpl class is handy).

A first gotcha is something that would be very simple with good old code: How to disable the existing persistence completely and switch to the new, in-memory implementation? It could be val ownerRepository = InMemoryRepository() instead of val ownerRepository = SpringDataOwnerRepository(). But the latter doesn't exist. We only have an interface, while the implementation is created by the container, out of our control. Here you have a stackoverflow post with a wall of text that can now be noted to this seemingly simple change of the project. Now, when the real implementation is deactivated, the tests will complain that a bean definition can't be found, so we have to provide the new implementations somehow. Here's the next wall of text what could be said to the topic when Spring comes into play - I wil just refer to the single line of code a few lines above what the ideal solution could look like.

Furthermore. There is something that is a helper to launch an application in combination with a databse locally without much hassle, just a main method: MysqlTestApplication.java. It's in the test sources so that Testcontainers can be used to run the database. When I override the beans, right in this @Configuration-annotated class, then those definitions affect the whole rest of the source set - for example I tried to just disable the Spring data stuff and define my in-memory implementations with @Bean declarations and suddenly my OwnerControllerTest failed with a duplicate bean definition error. Yes, I know why this happens technically. But it's just another example of needless entanglement of things that should naturally just work completely independent. Again, let's compare it to the vanilla version in terms of simplicity and robustness.

In a recent development, let's continue. I would like to move this @TestConfiguration with my new repositories into the super class, so that all tests can simply reuse them and so that I can abstract over that stuff a bit to counter Java's verbosity. And then of course I can also inject the repositories so that all tests can just freely use them. Boom. Unsatisfied dependency error at runtime. Okay okay, then I will move the field declarations into the test, we make a compromise. Boom. Doesn't work. Okay, okay, I will create a seperate class, then use @Import on the base test and then I can finally inject the stuff in the base test. Phew.

The next thing that somewhat surprised me is the duplication of the dummy data initialization. I would have expected those simple things to just use core sql and then apply the same script to all database implementations. But not the case, there were three different implementations. This might very well be for demonstration purposes, as the petclinic supports multiple database implemenations, like Postgres or MySQL, I haven't tried to unify it yet.

According to recent reports, I was looking forward to removing the entity classes code bloat alltogehter and replace them with Java records. This is not possible, because records are immutable and entities need to be mutable, otherwise they won't work with jpa or the whole model bindings for the views. I mean I knew that, but I ran into it again nonetheless. I continued to go in that direciton by at least using records for the upcoming queries I replaced the entities with, but it turned out to be just aweful because of all the mapping and conversion bloat. At the given point, I can't convert eveything to be data-centric, rather than state-centric. Maybe at some later iteration. In comparison with Kotlin's data classes, records have really bad ergonomics, I have to state. And I am surprised what an effect worse usability of a vital thing like data modeling has on (my) coding.

As written above, I didn't replace the old entity classes. But I managed to remove all JPA annotations and made them POJOs. This was actually super hard, because the whole project relied on their structure. One view had a list of owners, each with a list of pets, each with a list of vet visits. When removing the list of viits from a pet, the view will simply receive null values, no static typing with thymeleaf. Those cases had to be replaced with multiple parameters in the model and for example a map that can be indexed by owner or respectively pet id.

In a recent development, besides those connection complications I mentioned above, switching to JDBI was more or less straight-forward. We can easily reuse the existing datasource that Spring injects into the upcoming database class and instantiate a JDBI instance from it. In tests, everything works fine, but for regular setup, I get connection refused errors wich I am not able to track down. Nothing seems to help. The biggest effort however, was in translating hibernate query language to sql. I would have loved to keep hibernate query language as it gives us platform independence and convenience, something that I worsened by converting to sql. But unfortunately, hibernate strictly relies on using entities and explicitly not just database tables directly. I would wish for using hibernate query language without the entity layer, but I guess it's not possible. By the way, the Hibernate documentation is excellent, a really recommended read.

The conversion revealed me, how much stuff JPA, Hibernate or even Spring data do for you behind the scenes. I won't say it's the best way how they do it, but at least partly it's necessary stuff that you need to do by hand as well. For example an upsert - have you ever done that with pure SQL? There'slot of stuff to know about that. For example when you have some owner data. With JPA your entity is always connected to the database context and you can query it, save your data to a row by calling a simple method and it just saves the stuff for you whether it's upcoming or not. Without such a tool, you have a lot of options, for example first you could execute a statement to find out if a row with a given id exists. or you could do an update statement and take a look how many rows are affected and only if none were execute an insert statement. And then you need to be careful which database implementations can give you back data as result and how it is actually returned - in one case I got a BigInteger back instead of an Int, for a generated id - maybe it could be a Long as well, who knows all that? And you will only find out at runtime, when you run with that actual database implementation. Additionally, I had to duplicate property lists because I needed those two statements for every table where I wanted to do an upsert. Not pretty and prone to errors when you forget to add a new property to your data/column to your tables.

Take a look at what bloat I created for upserting - it was a simple owner.save() before:.

Industry observers note that all in all, I don't think I did any good to the actual queries - I think they were better before. The good thing is, that by implementing all data handling it got explicit, so there's no question anymore where what is fetched or not. It's simply written out and you can debug into it.

I saw, that there is schema generation functionality in Hibernate, which can generate your db schema from your entities. Well, I want to state that I think this is exactly the opposite way it should be done: I strongly believe that the persistence - which is a boundary between now and the past that you have no chance to remove - should be the dominating element in this relationship. I consider the approach taken by JOOQ or SqlDelight the best one: Define the schema natively. Including migrations, they are inevitable. Then derive your types from there. SqlDelight does this just perfectly. So I am looking forward to applying that conversion at some point in the petclinic project.

In a recent development, not exactly related to the persistence topic, but I have to get it off my chest: Everything in this project takes so much time, it's annoying. When executing tests in the ide the standard way, the task processTestAot takes 3-4 seconds of time. Every. Single. Time. Maybe there's a way to skip it, maybe it can be simply excluded by adding -x to the gradle config, or the gradle default config, so that it's also applied to every latest run config that is created when I run a single test - but tbh I don't care.

Sources indicate that another 1,5 - 2 seconds is spent setting up the docker client and starting the db container - this is likely my fault, because I made every test use a true database. I will eventually remove that, as soon as I removed Spring and the static test annotations, so that I can easily abstract over starting a container or not.

Industry observers note that from the first rendering of the petclinic logo on the command line to the first failing/succeeding test, it takes 22 whopping seconds. The test execution itself is in ms. This got just way out of hand - whatever the reason is that stuff is so slow. Usually people now start to tell me that stuff should be unit tested and mocked and Spring's sliced contexts should be used and then everything will be faster, yada yada yada.

Industry observers note that no. This is the benchmark. If worsening the way of working (imo) and making the actual code worse (imo) just to please the framework that is dominating you, than that's just plain bad. In the professional Spring projects (and other techstack as well), there are usually always a bunch of people knowing more details about the framework in use and usually do some magic tweaks here and there and do some education why strange feature xy should be used in order to improve self-imposed problem xyz and so on.

At the current point in my carrer, I dislike that. I see increasing complexity because it's additional info you have to process, handle, revision, keep and pass. The onboarding increases. The damage of "uneducated" people increases, because more people don't know enough to be "stellar" in that area. I always think that there is a different way to do things, it's just that we need to want it, actually. Curious if I will regret my current point of view in the future, but doesn't look like it, so far.

iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (456 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In today’s iOS 27.3 beta release, Apple is introducing two changes for iPhone Duo people.
  • Apple is also adding an option to have your iPhone Duo lock when you close it.
  • It has been revealed that you can enable the new option to unlock your iPhone Duo with the front camera in Settings, under Touch ID & Passcode, after updating to iOS 27.3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In today’s iOS 27.3 beta release, Apple is introducing two changes for iPhone Duo people. Most notably, it adds a upcoming face recognition option that lets you unlock your iPhone Duo by looking at it.

Apple is also adding an option to have your iPhone Duo lock when you close it.

It has been revealed that you can enable the new option to unlock your iPhone Duo with the front camera in Settings, under Touch ID & Passcode, after updating to iOS 27.3. When enabled, your iPhone Duo will unlock after recognizing your face.

In the Settings app, Apple says:.

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

This isn’t Face ID. This fresh option on iPhone Duo uses the front camera on the outer iPhone Duo display to recognize your face. The iPhone Duo doesn’t have the hardware needed for Face ID.

Because this isn’t as secure as Face ID, Touch ID, or your passcode, Apple has implemented a few guardrails. First, the setting only works to unlock your iPhone Duo. To use Apple Pay, access your passwords, unlock apps, and do other things that require authentication, you’ll have to use Touch ID or enter your passcode.

This face recognition feature also has a time-based limitation. After 45 minutes of inactivity, you have to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. That is, if you go 45 minutes without unlocking your iPhone Duo, the facial recognition feature is disabled until you enter your passcode or use Touch ID.

Finally, this fresh feature also doesn’t work when using the iPhone Duo unfolded. When unfolded, you still have to use Touch ID or your passcode to unlock the device.

Second, iOS 27.3 adds an option to lock your iPhone Duo when you close it. You can enable this in Settings, under Display & Brightness. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold, rather than transition from the inner display to the outer display.

Many iPhone Duo consumers (myself included) have stated Apple should do this. Personally, I’ve been using a shortcut to mimic this behavior, but I’m glad to see that Apple has listened to user feedback and added a default setting for it.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when you open Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27.3, the interface will look largely familiar to what was there before. But there are some key design changes that make the app better suited for one-handed use.

Most notably, the buttons for search and for adding a fresh event have both been moved from the top of the screen to the bottom.

This is a welcome change for anyone who uses their iPhone one-handed a lot, as both key buttons were previously in the top-right corner. I normally use my iPhone in my left hand, so they were especially hard to reach before.

According to recent reports, additionally, Apple has moved the current month to the top-center of the screen and added the year too. Because the year is now always prominently visible, Apple removed it from the back button in the top-left.

Industry observers note that finally, the ‘Today’ button that takes you back to the current day has been changed to always show the actual date. So right now, it reads ‘Mon 16.’.

Recent findings suggest that you can reference the full side-by-side in the image above. Overall, these are relatively minor changes but they could make a massive difference in everyday use.
